proofs.proof_tex:
Fix a finite set \(F\subset\mathcal U\) and a realization of an admissible band \(C\).  Write
\[
 \mathcal A_F(C)=\bigl\{u\in F:\Psi_{\theta_0}(u,t)\in C(t)
                    \text{ for every }t\in\mathcal D\bigr\},
 \qquad
 \mathcal L(C)=\sup_{t\in\mathcal D}\operatorname{diam}C(t).
\]
The events in this finite definition are measurable by the simultaneous-coverage requirement in Definition \(\mathrm{def:local\mbox{-}band\mbox{-}class}\).  If \(u,u'\in\mathcal A_F(C)\), then both \(\Psi_{\theta_0}(u,t)\) and \(\Psi_{\theta_0}(u',t)\) belong to the interval \(C(t)\) for every \(t\).  Hence
\[
 |\Psi_{\theta_0}(u,t)-\Psi_{\theta_0}(u',t)|
 \leq \operatorname{diam}C(t),
 \qquad
 d_\Psi(u,u')\leq\mathcal L(C).
\]
Taking the maximum over the finite accepted set proves
\[
 c\bigl(\mathcal A_F(C)\bigr)\leq\mathcal L(C).
\]
Moreover, for each \(u\in F\), the event \(u\in\mathcal A_F(C)\) is exactly the event that the entire curve indexed by \(u\) is covered.  Thus passing from the band to its accepted subset preserves every pointwise-in-parameter simultaneous-coverage probability.

Conversely, let a possibly randomized measurable rule select a subset \(A\subseteq F\).  For \(A\neq\varnothing\), define
\[
 C_A(t)=
 \left[\min_{u\in A}\Psi_{\theta_0}(u,t),
       \max_{u\in A}\Psi_{\theta_0}(u,t)\right].
\]
The endpoints are measurable because they are extrema over a finite set.  Every selected curve is covered, and finiteness of \(A\) permits interchange of the two maxima:
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \sup_{t\in\mathcal D}\operatorname{diam}C_A(t)
 &=\sup_{t\in\mathcal D}\max_{u,u'\in A}
      |\Psi_{\theta_0}(u,t)-\Psi_{\theta_0}(u',t)|\\
 &=\max_{u,u'\in A}\sup_{t\in\mathcal D}
      |\Psi_{\theta_0}(u,t)-\Psi_{\theta_0}(u',t)|
 =c_A.
 \end{aligned}
\]
For \(A=\varnothing\), take any fixed singleton interval; its diameter and the stipulated value \(c_A\) are both zero.  Randomization is retained as part of the subset rule, so this construction does not restrict the shape or randomization of the original class.

Now suppose that \(F\) is a \(\delta\)-net and that
\[
 \sup_{t\in\mathcal D}|\Psi_{\theta_0}(u,t)-
       \Psi_{\theta_0}(u_i,t)|\leq K_u\delta
\]
whenever \(u_i\in F\) is a nearest net point to \(u\).  Pad every nonempty envelope by \(K_u\delta\) at both endpoints.  If \(u_i\) is selected, the displayed inequality shows that the padded band covers the entire curve indexed by \(u\).  Its maximum width is at most \(c_A+2K_u\delta\).  This is the asserted deterministic transport from a net to \(\mathcal U\); the probability loss caused by replacing the law at \(u_i\) by the law at \(u\) is handled separately by total variation in the theorem.

It remains to establish computability of \(d_\Psi\).  Lemma \(\mathrm{lem:local\mbox{-}risk\mbox{-}map}\) states that \(\Psi_{\theta_0}\) is continuous and affine on each of finitely many polyhedral critical-cone cells.  Fix \(u,u'\).  For every pair of cells that can respectively contain \((u,t)\) and \((u',t)\), their intersection with the query restrictions has the form
\[
 \mathcal T_{ab}=\left\{t:A_{ab}t\leq b_{ab},\ 
 \mathbf 1^{\prime}t=0,\ t_k\geq0\text{ if }(v_0)_k=0,\
 \lVert t\rVert_2\leq L_0\right\}.
\]
On this set the curve difference is affine, say
\(\Psi_{\theta_0}(u,t)-\Psi_{\theta_0}(u',t)=\beta_{ab}+\gamma_{ab}^{\prime}t\).  Therefore its absolute maximum on \(\mathcal T_{ab}\) is the larger of the two second-order-cone program values
\[
 \max_{t}\ \sigma(\beta_{ab}+\gamma_{ab}^{\prime}t)
 \quad\text{subject to }t\in\mathcal T_{ab},
 \qquad \sigma\in\{-1,1\}.
\]
The feasible set is compact, so each maximum is attained.  Taking the maximum over the finitely many nonempty cell pairs and the two signs gives exactly \(d_\Psi(u,u')\).  On shared boundaries the affine formulas agree because the strongly convex critical-cone quadratic program has a unique minimizer; hence using closed cell systems neither omits nor changes a boundary value.  This proves all assertions.

Put \(I=I(\theta_0)\), \(q=1-\alpha\), \(P_u=N(u,I^{-1})\), and
\[
 \mathcal L(C)=\sup_{t\in\mathcal D}\operatorname{diam}C(Z,t).
\]
By Lemma \(\mathrm{lem:local\mbox{-}risk\mbox{-}map}\), the function \(\Psi_{\theta_0}\) is continuous and affine on finitely many polyhedral cells.  On a line segment in \(\mathcal U\), partition the segment at its finitely many cell crossings and sum the affine increments.  If \(K_u\) is the maximum operator norm of the coefficient of \(u\) among these affine pieces, this gives
\[
 \sup_{t\in\mathcal D}|\Psi_{\theta_0}(u,t)-
 \Psi_{\theta_0}(u',t)|\leq K_u\lVert u-u'\rVert_2.
\]
The constant is finite because there are finitely many pieces.  Consequently
\[
 D_\star=\sup_{u,u'\in\mathcal U}d_\Psi(u,u')
 \leq 2K_uM<\infty.
\]

We first bound the two approximation errors.  Whitening the two equal-covariance Gaussian laws and integrating in the one likelihood-ratio direction gives
\[
 \operatorname{TV}(P_u,P_{u_i})
 =2\Phi\!\left(\frac{\lVert I^{1/2}(u-u_i)\rVert_2}{2}\right)-1.
\]
Since the derivative of the right-hand side as a function of its norm argument is at most \(1/\sqrt{2\pi}\), every \(\delta\)-net satisfies
\[
 \epsilon_\delta
 \leq \frac{\lVert I^{1/2}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\delta}{\sqrt{2\pi}}.
\]

For observation quantization, let \(P_0=N(0,I^{-1})\).  On every bounded cell \(o\), use the parameter-independent reconstruction kernel \(P_0(\,\cdot\mid o)\); use any fixed probability kernel on the tail cell.  The likelihood ratio is
\[
 \ell_u(z)=\frac{dP_u}{dP_0}(z)
 =\exp\!\left(u^{\prime}Iz-\frac12u^{\prime}Iu\right).
\]
If a bounded cell has diameter at most \(h\), then
\[
 \sup_{z,z'\in o}|\log\ell_u(z)-\log\ell_u(z')|
 \leq \lVert I\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}Mh.
\]
Because the conditional likelihood ratio is \(\ell_u(z)/E_0[\ell_u(Z)\mid Z\in o]\), it lies between the minimum and maximum of \(\ell_u\) on the cell after normalization.  Thus the conditional total variation from the reconstruction law is at most
\(\exp(\lVert I\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}Mh)-1\).  Also, for \(R>M\), a coordinatewise Gaussian tail bound and a union bound give
\[
 \tau_R:=\sup_{\lVert u\rVert_2\leq M}
 P_u\{Z\notin[-R,R]^q\}
 \leq 2q\exp\!\left{-\frac{(R-M)^2}
 {2\lambda_{\max}(I^{-1})}\right}.
\]
Consequently, if \(\widetilde P_u\) denotes the law obtained by quantizing and reconstructing,
\[
 \sup_{u\in\mathcal U}\operatorname{TV}(P_u,\widetilde P_u)
 \leq \epsilon_h:=\min\left\{1,
 e^{\lVert I\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}Mh}-1+\tau_R\right\}.
\]
This is an explicit deficiency bound.  It tends to zero if \(R\to\infty\) and \(h\to0\); in particular this holds when \(R\to\infty\) and \(hR\to0\).

We next prove the lower certificate for an arbitrary externally randomized measurable band \(C\in\mathfrak C_{1-\alpha}\).  Apply Proposition \(\mathrm{prop:curve\mbox{-}decision\mbox{-}reduction}\) to \(F=\mathcal U_N\) and let \(A\) be the resulting accepted subset.  Pointwise,
\[
 c_A\leq\mathcal L(C),
\]
and under \(P_{u_i}\), the inclusion probability of \(i\) is at least \(q\).  Quantize, reconstruct with the preceding kernel, and then apply the accepted-subset rule, including its original external randomization.  Conditional on a cell \(o\), this produces probabilities \(x_{oA}\).  Total variation and \(0\leq c_A\leq D_\star\) imply, for every \(i\),
\[
 \sum_o p_{io}\sum_{A\ni i}x_{oA}\geq q-\epsilon_h,
 \qquad
 \sum_o p_{io}\sum_Ac_Ax_{oA}
 \leq E_{u_i}[\mathcal L(C)]+D_\star\epsilon_h.
\]
The first equality constraint \(\sum_Ax_{oA}=1\) holds by construction.  Hence this rule is feasible for the finite program at coverage \(q-\epsilon_h\), with risk bounded by
\(\sup_uE_u[\mathcal L(C)]+D_\star\epsilon_h\).  Taking first the infimum over \(C\) and then rearranging yields
\[
 V_{N,h}(q-\epsilon_h)-D_\star\epsilon_h
 \leq L_\alpha(\theta_0,v_0;M,L_0).
\]

For the upper certificate, take a finite-program rule feasible at coverage \(q+\epsilon_\delta\), with objective within an arbitrary \(\eta>0\) of \(V_{N,h}(q+\epsilon_\delta)\).  If it selects a nonempty \(A\), output
\[
 C_A^\delta(t)=
 \left[\min_{i\in A}\Psi_{\theta_0}(u_i,t)-K_u\delta,
       \max_{i\in A}\Psi_{\theta_0}(u_i,t)+K_u\delta\right],
\]
and output a fixed singleton if \(A=\varnothing\).  Given \(u\in\mathcal U\), select a nearest \(u_i\) with \(\lVert u-u_i\rVert_2\leq\delta\), breaking ties deterministically.  When \(i\in A\), the Lipschitz bound proves simultaneous coverage of the curve indexed by \(u\).  Therefore
\[
 P_u\{\Psi_{\theta_0}(u,t)\in C_A^\delta(t)
       \text{ for every }t\in\mathcal D\}
 \geq P_{u_i}\{i\in A\}-\operatorname{TV}(P_u,P_{u_i})
 \geq q.
\]
The resulting band belongs to \(\mathfrak C_{1-\alpha}\).  Its loss is at most \(c_A+2K_u\delta\), and another total-variation comparison gives
\[
 \sup_{u\in\mathcal U}E_u[\mathcal L(C_A^\delta)]
 \leq V_{N,h}(q+\epsilon_\delta)+\eta
       +D_\star\epsilon_\delta+2K_u\delta.
\]
Letting \(\eta\downarrow0\) proves the upper displayed inequality in the theorem.

For completeness, we prove rather than assume equality of the displayed finite primal and dual values.  Weak duality follows by multiplying the coverage constraints by \(\ell_i\geq0\), the risk constraints by \(\pi_i\geq0\), and the normalization constraints by unrestricted \(\eta_o\).  The resulting Lagrangian is
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 &\zeta\left(1-\sum_i\pi_i\right)
 +q\sum_i\ell_i+\sum_o\eta_o\\
 &\quad+\sum_{o,A}x_{oA}
 \left(c_A\sum_i\pi_ip_{io}
       -\sum_{i\in A}\ell_ip_{io}-\eta_o\right).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Its infimum over unrestricted \(\zeta\) and \(x_{oA}\geq0\) is finite exactly under the dual constraints in Definition \(\mathrm{def:finite\mbox{-}decision\mbox{-}program}\).

To obtain the reverse inequality by a finite-dimensional argument, fix \(\gamma<V_{N,h}(q)\).  Let \(\mathcal X\) be the product of the finitely many subset-probability simplices, and denote grid coverage and risk by
\[
 a_i(x)=\sum_op_{io}\sum_{A\ni i}x_{oA},
 \qquad
 b_i(x)=\sum_op_{io}\sum_Ac_Ax_{oA}.
\]
The compact convex set
\[
 \mathcal K=\{((q-a_i(x))_i,(b_i(x)-\gamma)_i):x\in\mathcal X\}
\]
does not meet the nonpositive orthant.  Choose a closest pair between \(\mathcal K\) and that orthant.  Projection onto the orthant and the elementary first-order inequality for squared Euclidean distance yield nonnegative vectors \(\ell,\pi\), not both zero, such that
\[
 \sum_i\ell_i\{q-a_i(x)\}
 +\sum_i\pi_i\{b_i(x)-\gamma\}>0
 \quad\text{for every }x\in\mathcal X.
\]
The full-set action has \(a_i=1\geq q\) for every \(i\), so \(\sum_i\pi_i>0\).  Divide both multiplier vectors by this positive sum.  Then \(\sum_i\pi_i=1\), and minimizing the last display over each simplex row separately shows that the choices
\[
 \eta_o=min_A\left\{c_A\sum_i\pi_ip_{io}
             -\sum_{i\in A}\ell_ip_{io}\right\}
\]
are dual feasible and have objective strictly larger than \(\gamma\).  Since this holds for every \(\gamma<V_{N,h}(q)\), weak duality proves equality.  Thus primal feasible solutions and dual feasible solutions provide checkable certificates on the two sides.

It remains to show that the certificates converge and are implementable.  Because \(\epsilon_h\leq q\) and \(\epsilon_\delta\leq\alpha\), both coverage arguments \(q-\epsilon_h\) and \(q+\epsilon_\delta\) lie in \([0,1]\).  Mix an optimal rule at level \(q-\epsilon_h\) with the rule that always selects the full net, using probability
\[
 \beta=\frac{\epsilon_\delta+\epsilon_h}{\alpha+\epsilon_h}\in[0,1].
\]
The mixture has coverage at least \(q+\epsilon_\delta\) and increases every expected cost by at most \(D_\star\beta\).  Hence
\[
 V_{N,h}(q+\epsilon_\delta)-V_{N,h}(q-\epsilon_h)
 \leq D_\star\frac{\epsilon_\delta+\epsilon_h}
                         {\alpha+\epsilon_h}.
\]
Combining this inequality with the two certificates bounds their gap by
\[
 D_\star\left\{
 \frac{\epsilon_\delta+\epsilon_h}{\alpha+\epsilon_h}
 +\epsilon_\delta+\epsilon_h\right\}+2K_u\delta,
\]
which tends to zero under \(\delta\to0\), \(R\to\infty\), and \(hR\to0\).

Every input to the finite program admits a certified finite computation.  Proposition \(\mathrm{prop:curve\mbox{-}decision\mbox{-}reduction}\) supplies finitely many second-order-cone programs for each \(c_A\); primal and conic-dual feasible points give lower and upper numerical enclosures.  On \([-R,R]^q\), the Gaussian density and its derivatives are explicit and uniformly bounded for \(u_i\in\mathcal U\), so interval quadrature on successively refined cells encloses each \(p_{io}\); the displayed \(\tau_R\) encloses the omitted tail.  Replacing probabilities and costs by outward endpoints and padding each coverage row by its total probability enclosure error gives finite robust linear programs whose lower and upper values bracket the exact program.  Probability errors perturb an inclusion probability by at most their rowwise total error, while uniform cost errors and the same rowwise error perturb risk by at most the cost error plus \(D_\star\) times the probability error.  Thus these numerical brackets converge as the quadrature and conic enclosure errors vanish.

Choose any sequence of meshes and numerical enclosures satisfying the stated limits, and use the upper-program optimizer in the padded-envelope construction above.  Its worst expected maximum width converges to \(L_\alpha(\theta_0,v_0;M,L_0)\) by the vanishing certificate gap, so these bands are asymptotically minimax among all externally randomized measurable interval-section bands.  If \(D_\star=0\), all curves coincide; the singleton band containing that common curve has coverage one and width zero, proving the conclusion directly.
